analysis.one_liner: Extends all copyright terms by 20 years and exempts small businesses from music licensing fees.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the bill; 20 days after it was introduced, the identical Senate bill was signed into law, adding 20 years to every copyright.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would add 20 years to every copyright — from the author's life plus 50 years to life plus 70, and up to 95 years for corporate "works made for hire" — so works by long-dead creators would stay under private control two more decades. Its second title would let small restaurants, bars, and shops play radio and TV music without paying the licensing fees that compensate songwriters. The House never voted on this version; instead, the Senate passed the identical bill and it became law the same month.
analysis.who_benefits: Holders of long-existing copyrights — film studios, music publishers, record labels, and the heirs of famous authors — would collect exclusive royalties for an extra 20 years on works already created, including works scheduled to enter the public domain. Small restaurants, bars, and retailers under the size limits would stop paying music licensing fees on radio and TV play, and small proprietors would gain a court process to challenge the rates they are charged. Libraries would get a narrow new right to preserve works in the last 20 years of their copyright term.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Film studios, music publishers, restaurants and bars

how_it_helps.text: Owners of existing copyrights — including film studios, music publishers, and record labels — would keep exclusive rights for 20 more years on works already created, some dating to the 1920s, and would extend sound-recording protections to 2067.
Restaurants, bars, and stores under the square-footage limits could play radio and TV broadcasts without paying performing-rights licensing fees, cutting a real operating cost for small businesses.
Small proprietors would win a court process to challenge license rates set by performing rights societies like ASCAP and BMI, with the going industry rate presumed reasonable in the meantime.
Authors and their heirs would gain new termination rights allowing them to reclaim old renewal-term licenses and renegotiate them during the extended term.

analysis.who_pays: The public: novels, films, songs, and artwork that were scheduled to become free for anyone to reprint, adapt, or preserve would stay locked up for an extra 20 years. Songwriters and composers lose licensing fees from the newly exempt establishments — their royalties are the small businesses' savings. Libraries, teachers, filmmakers, and independent creators would wait decades longer to use 20th-century works.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, libraries, and working songwriters

drawbacks.text: The term extension is retroactive: it rewards owners of works created decades earlier and does nothing to encourage new creation. Works from the 1920s and 1930s that were about to enter the public domain — free for anyone to copy, screen, or adapt — would instead stay private property until 2019 and beyond.

The small-business music exemption is paid for by songwriters and composers, whose income depends on performance royalties from restaurants, bars, and retail play; a proprietor who wrongly claims the exemption and loses in court would owe double the unpaid license fees for up to three years.

The library and archives preservation exception is narrow: it applies only to works in the final 20 years of their term, and only if the work is not commercially exploited and no copy is available at a reasonable price.

The 'sense of the Congress' asking copyright owners to share the 20 added years of royalties with the screenwriters, directors, and performers who made the films is a non-binding statement with no enforcement behind it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are large and permanent for copyright owners and modest and genuine for small businesses, but the costs fall broadly on everyone else. Because the extension applies to works already created, the public gives up 20 more years of access to its own cultural heritage in exchange for no new works; the bill's public-interest pieces — a narrow library exception and an unenforceable plea to share royalties with screenwriters and performers — do not offset that. The small-business licensing relief is real help for Main Street, but it comes directly out of songwriters' pay.

outcome.mechanism: The House never voted on it — three weeks after introduction, the identical Senate bill was signed into law, so this version was set aside and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Sensenbrenner introduced the bill on October 7, 1998, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day.
On October 15, 1998, the bill was sent to the Subcommittee on Courts and Intellectual Property, where it stayed — no hearings, no markup, no floor vote.

The same day, the record posted a note — 'For Further Action See S.505' — pointing to the Senate companion, which carried the same two titles: the Sonny Bono Copyright Term Extension Act and the Fairness in Music Licensing Act of 1998.

Congress moved the substance through the Senate instead: the companion bill was signed into law on October 27, 1998, as Public Law 105-298, and this House version died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of valuable old copyrights came out ahead: the identical Senate bill became law, giving film studios, music publishers, and authors' heirs 20 extra years of exclusive royalties on works already made. Small restaurants and bars also gained the music licensing exemption; songwriters and the public domain came out behind.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Major copyright holders and small business owners

for.name: F. James Sensenbrenner Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on October 7, 1998, combining the copyright term extension with the small-business music licensing exemption.

for.name: Bill McCollum
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor; the bill was referred to the intellectual property subcommittee eight days later.

for.name: Film studios, music publishers, and record labels (the copyright industries)
for.role: Industry groups behind the copyright term extension
for.what_they_did: Pressed Congress for a 20-year extension of existing copyrights as major early-20th-century works approached the public domain; the extension is Title I of the bill.

against.name: Songwriters and performing rights organizations (ASCAP, BMI)
against.what_they_did: Opposed the music licensing exemption that would let restaurants, bars, and shops play their members' music without paying performance royalties.

against.name: Librarians, archivists, and public-domain advocates
against.role: Custodians of and advocates for public access to creative works
against.what_they_did: Warned that extending existing terms locked up 20th-century works and delayed public access; no member of Congress moved to stop the Senate version.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken on this bill and its action history shows no recorded opposition; the Republican sponsor and cosponsor were joined by no Democrats on paper, but the identical Senate bill cleared both chambers and was signed by a Democratic president within three weeks.

industries.industry: Film studios and large copyright holders (music and book publishers, record labels)
industries.note: Title I adds 20 years to every existing copyright, a direct windfall to owners of works already created — the extension's entire value comes from works the public would otherwise get for free. This is the bill's headline provision and the reason it became law.

The music licensing exemption lets small establishments play their music without paying performance royalties, shrinking songwriters' income; the term extension does not help working creators of existing works, and the promise to share the extra royalties with film writers, directors, and performers is non-binding.

Establishments under the size limits (3,750 square feet for food and drink venues) would stop paying ASCAP/BMI-style fees for radio and TV play, and small proprietors would get a rate-court process. The savings are real but are subtracted from songwriters' royalties.

The bill grants a new right to reproduce and share works digitally in the last 20 years of their term for preservation and scholarship — but the same bill pushes that window 20 years further into the future for every work, so the net effect on public access is negative.
The exemption removes a slice of their licensing base and new rules force rate determinations and interim escrow payments for small proprietors who challenge their fees.
